title: Prompt-to-Game 已到来：哪些平台有望胜出？
content:
Prompt-to-Game Is Here. Which Platforms Are Positioned to Win?
Skip to content
AI x Gaming
Prompt-to-Game Is Here. Which Platforms Are Positioned to Win?
By Matthew Camp •   October 27, 2026
AI game creation on mobile | Source:
Roblox
,
Google
,
Meta
Between July and October 2026, Roblox, Meta, and Google each unveiled a product that lets users make a playable game from a text prompt:
Roblox Build
,
Meta Horizon Create
, and
Google Playground
. They join startups such as
Astrocade
,
Rosebud
, and
Jabali
in prompt-based game creation.
Today, we are examining why these companies are investing in prompt-based game creation now and what each stands to gain. We’ll look at how these tools connect to their existing products and audiences, and whether creators and players are showing early signs of traction. Finally, we’ll lay out where the ecosystem may be heading and which platforms appear best positioned to benefit.
From UGC to Prompt-to-Game
User-generated content (UGC) platforms, where players publish games for others to play, have never lacked games. Epic reported
325,000+ active games in Fortnite
, and Super Mario Maker 2 players had uploaded
more than 26M courses
by May 2021. Until now, aspiring creators had two options. They could use a full tool, such as Roblox Studio or Unreal Editor for Fortnite, to make almost anything, but they needed to code and use a computer. Or they could use an in-game editor, such as Super Mario Maker, to easily build new levels, but they were constrained by the game’s rules and mechanics.
AI model improvements have largely removed that trade-off. From a single text prompt, users can create a complete game, including code, art, and sound, on a phone or in a browser, without the fixed rules of an in-game editor. Naavik covered these emerging prompt tools when
Astrocade raised $56M
in May. As of October 2026, every platform tested produced a playable game in under 20 minutes.
Even so, the games tend to be bite-sized experiences closer to hypercasual games. This largely reflects the limits of today’s models. Horizon lead Saxs Persson
said AI generation starts to drift
after the first ten or so prompts, which makes larger games hard to build through prompts alone. Until that changes, prompt-made games may struggle to become deep, content-heavy games that keep players returning.
Each company behind these platforms has its own reason to invest. For Roblox and Meta, prompt tools give new, casual creators a way to make content for their current audiences. Roblox said any one of its 132M daily active users
“could come up with the next hit game
,” and Build games enter the same ranking as every other Roblox game. Meta’s Horizon Create will
publish games directly into Facebook, Instagram, and Horizon feeds
. Google labels Playground
an experiment
, hasn’t said how it would generate revenue, and lets players play its games only on Playground. For Astrocade, which counts
Google’s AI Futures Fund among its investors
, the platform is the core business, so it has to build its audience from scratch.
Every AI platform evaluated for this article offers blank-prompt creation, and most default to it. Some also offer templates or remix, letting players create a new game from another user’s game.
Comparison of AI game-creation platforms, October 2026 | Source: Company materials, Naavik
Creators Follow Players
Early evidence suggests these tools are reaching people outside the existing developer base. During Roblox Build’s New Zealand alpha,
71% of users who created a game had never used Roblox Studio
. Most of these platforms also let people create games on a phone, opening UGC creation to mobile-first markets.
Reaching new creators is the first step, but keeping them requires incentives. Roblox Build creators can earn Robux through Roblox’s
Creator Rewards
program, which pays based on engagement from paying players. Astrocade offers payouts from a
$10M creator fund
, and Meta has announced a
creator fund
for Horizon. As more platforms seek new creators, they will compete to attract and retain the best creators, those who bring players back to their games. Creator funds help jumpstart creation, but over time players fund payouts through ads or in-app purchases. Roblox already funds payouts through ads, while Astrocade doesn’t yet support ads or in-app purchases.
More Games Don’t Mean More Play
While these platforms need to appeal to creators, the bigger test is winning over players, and most of the products evaluated lead with play. Google’s Playground opens on a feed of editors’ picks, Astrocade opens on its game feed, and Meta’s games are
built to run in Facebook and Instagram feeds
. The approach borrows from social media, where anyone can publish to a large audience and a feed decides what users see.
However, more games don’t necessarily mean more play, because UGC platforms concentrate play in hits. Roblox’s top 1,000 experiences accounted for roughly 80% of in-experience hours in
2024
and
2025
, and visibility largely relies on its discovery algorithm.
Share of in-experience hours by experience rank, 2024 (top) and 2025 (bottom) | Source: Roblox
FY2024
and
FY2025
10-Ks
AI-made games rely on the same kind of discovery systems to reach players. Roblox ranks games
by retention
, Meta says
reach will depend on whether players come back
, and Google’s Playground
ranks games by plays and likes
.
Quality is the other half of the problem. Fixed rules in in-game editors made quality checks possible. For example,
Super Mario Maker
and Geometry Dash require creators to beat their own level before publishing it. AI-made games have no such rules. Two of the new AI platforms check games before listing them publicly. Google’s Playground runs “a quick test for playability, stability, and safety,” and Astrocade’s team reviews games before they enter its feed. Roblox Build’s check covers
safety
, and
Meta describes its review in safety terms
. These checks evaluate whether games are safe and
